title: Making the nitronium ion
subtitle: Sulfuric acid turns nitric acid into NO₂⁺

acids.caption: nitric acid + sulfuric acid
acids.learnerPrompt: Sulfuric acid is the stronger acid. Protonate nitric acid where it will help a leaving group form.
hintTiers: Which oxygen of nitric acid, once protonated, could leave as a neutral molecule?
Protonate the OH oxygen: it then carries H₂O⁺, a good leaving group. Two arrows: a lone pair takes the proton, and the O–H bond of H₂SO₄ breaks.
O4 lone pair → H6 (new O4–H6 bond); O7–H6 σ bond → lone pair on O7.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Sulfuric acid is the stronger acid (pKa about −3 against −1.4), so it gives its proton to nitric acid, not the other way round.
That oxygen can be protonated, but it gives no leaving group. Protonate the OH, so water can leave.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: O4 takes the proton. H6 now has two bonds: which bond of sulfuric acid must break?

protonated-nitric-acid.caption: protonated nitric acid + hydrogen sulfate
protonated-nitric-acid.learnerPrompt: Water leaves. Draw how the nitronium ion forms.
hintTiers: Losing water from nitrogen would leave it short of electrons. Which neighbouring atom can donate a pair to nitrogen as it goes?
The O⁻ lone pair forms a second N=O π bond while the N–O bond to the H₂O⁺ breaks. Two arrows, at the same time.
O3 lone pair → π N2–O3; σ N2–O4 → lone pair on O4.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydrogen sulfate is a very weak nucleophile, and attacking nitrogen gives nothing useful. Let water leave first.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Water leaves, but this leaves N⁺ with only six electrons. Which lone pair can move in to form a second N=O?

steps.explanationAfterStep: Protonating the OH turns it into H₂O⁺, a good leaving group. (In concentrated acid, the water is protonated in turn by a second H₂SO₄.)
NO₂⁺ is linear, O=N⁺=O, and isoelectronic with CO₂. Its nitrogen is the electrophilic atom that the arene attacks.

mechanismSummary: Sulfuric acid, the stronger acid, protonates the OH of nitric acid. Water then leaves as the O⁻ lone pair forms a second N=O bond, giving the linear nitronium ion, NO₂⁺: the electrophile of nitration.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 21
